title: The Oak and the Reeds
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: An Oak that grew on the bank of a river was uprooted by a severe gale of wind, and thrown across the stream. It fell among some Reeds growing by the water, and said to them, "How is it that you, who are so frail and slender, have managed to weather the storm, whereas I, with all my strength, have been torn up by the roots and hurled into the river?" "You were stubborn," came the reply, "and fought against the storm, which proved stronger than you: but we bow and yield to every breeze, and thus the gale passed harmlessly over our heads."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what uproots the Oak?
options: A passing flood
A lightning strike
A severe gale of wind
A group of woodcutters

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Oak fall after being uprooted?
options: Among some Reeds growing by the water
Onto the far bank of the river
Across a narrow forest path
Into a deep ravine nearby

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Oak ask the Reeds?
options: Why they grow so close to the riverbank
Whether they saw the storm coming
How long they have lived by the river
How they managed to survive the storm despite being frail

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Reeds say the Oak did during the storm?
options: It bent low just as the Reeds did
It was stubborn and fought against the storm
It called out for help too late
It tried to shield the Reeds from the wind

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Reeds do instead of resisting the wind?
options: They grow taller each time the wind blows
They cling tightly to the riverbank
They bow and yield to every breeze
They spread their roots deeper into the soil

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Oak's great strength fail to save it?
options: Its rigid resistance to the storm is exactly what breaks it
It was already weakened by disease before the storm
It was struck at its weakest point by chance
It had grown too close to the water to be stable

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does bending in the wind help the Reeds survive?
options: It hides them from the worst of the wind entirely
It allows them to grow taller than the Oak
It lets them take root somewhere safer nearby
It lets the force of the storm pass over them instead of breaking them

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Reeds are "frail and slender"?
options: Tall and thickly rooted
Thin and delicate in appearance
Bright and colorful to look at
Ancient and slow to grow

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "yield" mean in "we bow and yield to every breeze"?
options: To grow rapidly in size
To break apart completely
To give way or bend rather than resist
To call out loudly for help

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Flexibility can survive hardship that rigid strength cannot
Trees are always weaker than the plants that grow near them
Storms are more dangerous near rivers than anywhere else
Only stubborn things are worth admiring

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the Oak originally grow?
options: At the top of a hill
Beside a stone wall
In the middle of a field
On the bank of a river

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Oak after it is uprooted?
options: It is carried far downstream by the current
It is thrown across the stream
It is left standing but leaning sideways
It is buried under fallen branches

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Oak say about its own strength?
options: That it never felt strong even before the storm
That its strength came from growing near the water
That it had all its strength, yet was still torn up by the roots
That it lost its strength slowly over many years

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is implied by the Reeds saying the storm "proved stronger than you"?
options: The Oak overestimated its ability to resist the storm
The storm was unusually powerful compared to past storms
The Reeds also nearly failed to survive the storm
The Oak had been weak for a long time before the storm

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Reeds' answer be considered a lesson for the Oak?
options: It proves that the Reeds are physically stronger than the Oak
It shows that the Reeds do not respect the Oak's strength
It suggests the Oak should have grown somewhere else entirely
It explains a different way of facing hardship that the Oak did not consider

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the gale passed "harmlessly" over the Reeds?
options: Without making any sound
Without causing any damage
Without being noticed at all
Without lasting very long

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A group of Reeds is uprooted while a nearby Oak survives unharmed
An Oak and some Reeds work together to withstand a storm
A mighty Oak is destroyed by a storm that the yielding Reeds survive
A storm passes without affecting either the Oak or the Reeds
